strengths: Novel and practically relevant reformulation of privacy-preserving video understanding: operating on frozen video foundation model latent features rather than raw pixels, avoiding costly retraining and enabling plug-and-play use with modern large VFMs (VideoMAE, V-JEPA, InternVideo).

First method to demonstrate privacy preservation across multiple heterogeneous downstream tasks (action recognition, temporal action detection, weakly-supervised anomaly detection) rather than being tailored to a single task, addressing a genuine limitation of prior pixel-level approaches (SPAct, TeD-SPAD).

Thoughtful loss design: clip-level self-supervised mutual-information-destroying objective, multi-task co-training, and a latent consistency loss specifically to prevent overfitting to seen proxy tasks and preserve generalization to unseen tasks -- supported by clear ablations (Tables 4, 5, 9).

Extensive experimental validation across five backbones of varying scale, multiple privacy/utility benchmarks, and thorough ablations (architecture choice, attention heads, training data scale, loss weighting), lending good empirical support to the core claims.

Practical efficiency benefits are well quantified: substantially fewer trainable parameters than baselines, faster training via precomputed frozen features, and favorable runtime-vs-performance curves (Fig. 4, Table 13).

Introduces new protocols to evaluate and partially mitigate gender presentation bias in action recognition, an underexplored area in video understanding, with results on both a controlled synthetic-bias benchmark (NTU) and a real-world imbalanced dataset (Toyota Smarthome).
weaknesses: Privacy evaluation is largely restricted to linear-probe attacks (VISPR cMAP, gait retrieval); there is no analysis against stronger/adaptive adversaries (e.g., nonlinear probes, adversaries aware of the AAM defense, or attempts to invert/reconstruct private attributes), which is important for validating true robustness of an anonymization method.

The core self-supervised privacy objective (minimizing similarity between static clip pairs to destroy shared spatial/private information) is conceptually a fairly direct extension of the mutual-information-based objective in Dave et al. (2022b)/Fioresi et al. (2023); the main technical novelty is the latent-space clip-level application plus the new consistency and multi-task losses, which is a reasonable but somewhat incremental algorithmic contribution.

Comparisons to prior pixel-level anonymization baselines (SPAct, TeD-SPAD, VITA) may be somewhat apples-to-oranges given the fundamentally different threat models (pixel vs. latent access), and the paper does not include other recent latent/feature-space privacy baselines if any exist, limiting the strength of the 'first' and 'outperforms' claims.

Gender bias evaluation uses a binary gender formulation (acknowledged by the authors as non-inclusive), and the bias mitigation appears to be a byproduct of the general privacy objective rather than an explicit, principled debiasing mechanism, so the generalizability of these bias results to other demographic attributes is unclear.

As explicitly acknowledged, the method cannot protect privacy if raw video must be transmitted/stored before feature extraction, which meaningfully restricts the real-world applicability of the framework to scenarios where feature extraction already happens on a trusted device.

Reported privacy leakage reduction percentages vary noticeably across backbones (e.g., 35.5% for I3D vs. ~29% for VideoMAE-B/VJEPA-H), and the headline '35%' figure in the abstract is not representative of results on the larger, more modern foundation models, which slightly overstates the generality of the main claim.

strengths: Introduces a genuinely useful reformulation of privacy-preserving video understanding by operating in the latent feature space of frozen video foundation models rather than at the pixel level, addressing a real practical limitation of prior task-specific, retraining-heavy approaches (SPAct, TeD-SPAD, Wu et al.).

The proposed AAM/SPLAVU framework is evaluated across a genuinely diverse set of downstream tasks (action recognition, temporal action detection, anomaly detection) and across multiple backbones of increasing scale (I3D, VideoMAE-B, VJEPA-H, InternVideo-H, VideoMAEv2-G), showing consistent trends and demonstrating scalability to large modern VFMs with minimal trainable parameters.

Extensive and thoughtful ablation studies (loss components, AAM architecture, attention head counts, task-subset generalization, training-set scale, latent-consistency weight) that clearly justify design choices and support the generalization claims.

Additional analyses beyond the core method are valuable and rigorous: black-box/white-box inversion attack resistance, qualitative reconstruction analysis, gait recognition as a temporal-attribute stress test, video retrieval generalization, and a training-compute/parameter-efficiency comparison.

The proposed gender-bias evaluation protocols (NTU-Bias-F/M and Toyota Smarthome) are a novel and well-motivated contribution to an understudied problem in video understanding, and the method shows a meaningful, non-trivial byproduct benefit in bias mitigation without an explicit debiasing objective.
weaknesses: The headline '35% reduction in privacy leakage' figure is only achieved on the I3D backbone; for the larger and arguably more relevant modern backbones (VideoMAE-B, VJEPA-H) the relative reduction is smaller (~29%) and absolute residual cMAP remains substantial (e.g., 49.92 and 51.42), suggesting privacy leakage is not fully mitigated at scale despite the abstract's framing.

Baseline comparisons against prior anonymization methods (SPAct, TeD-SPAD, Wu et al., downsampling/blurring/blackening) are only conducted on the older I3D backbone; there is no direct head-to-head comparison with these methods on the larger foundation-model backbones where SPLAVU's advantages are most emphasized, making the scaling claims partly asserted rather than directly benchmarked.

The framework is explicitly not robust to white-box inversion attacks, which the paper itself flags as an important unresolved limitation, leaving open questions about real-world deployment security when adversaries have model access.

The privacy evaluation relies primarily on a proxy classifier (cMAP via retrained attribute predictor), which, while standard in this literature, may not fully characterize residual leakage; stronger or more adaptive privacy attacks (beyond the inversion experiments) are not explored as thoroughly as they could be.

The gender-bias protocol explicitly relies on a binary gender formulation, acknowledged by the authors as not inclusive, limiting the generalizability of the bias-mitigation claims to more nuanced or diverse gender categorizations.

The method currently only supports global clip-level embedding tasks and explicitly cannot handle dense prediction tasks (segmentation, captioning, patch-wise embeddings), which somewhat narrows the claimed generality of 'video understanding' anonymization.

Some recent related privacy-preserving methods mentioned in related work (e.g., Peng et al. 2024) are not included as quantitative baselines, leaving the comparison set slightly dated relative to the field.
